units.t: The Age of Revolutions. Episode two.
In this episode: The fight to end slavery, 1848: the year Europe caught fire and The Russian Revolution.
Part one. The fight to end slavery.
For centuries, the trade in enslaved Africans was one of the world's biggest businesses.
Ending it took rebellion, protest and war.
The Atlantic slave trade.
European traders bought captives in West and Central Africa, often from African rulers and traders, and shipped them to work on plantations growing sugar, tobacco, cotton and coffee.
Around 12.
5 million people were embarked, and about 1.
8 million died on the brutal Middle Passage, chained below deck for weeks.
Brazil and the Caribbean received the largest share.
The Atlantic system was unprecedented in scale and in being based on race.
Enslaved people had no legal rights and could be bought, sold, beaten and separated from families.
They resisted by slowing work, running away, preserving culture and language, and open revolt.
Maroon communities in Jamaica defended their freedom for generations.
The Haitian Revolution.
Saint-Domingue, a French colony, was the world's richest sugar colony, worked by around half a million enslaved people.
In August 1791 they launched a massive uprising.
Led by figures such as Toussaint Louverture, a formerly enslaved man and brilliant general, they fought French, Spanish and British forces.
When Napoleon sent a large army to restore control, it was defeated, weakened by yellow fever and fierce resistance.
In 1804 the colony declared independence as Haiti: the first nation founded by formerly enslaved people, and the only successful large-scale slave revolt in history.
France later forced Haiti to pay a crippling indemnity.
The British campaign.
A mass movement grew in Britain from the 1780s, driven early by Quakers.
Formerly enslaved writers like Olaudah Equiano told their own stories.
Thomas Clarkson gathered evidence, and William Wilberforce led the fight in Parliament for about 20 years.
Hundreds of thousands signed petitions, many boycotted slave-grown sugar, and a diagram of the slave ship Brookes shocked the public.
Britain banned the trade in 1807.
That freed no one already enslaved.
After a major uprising in Jamaica in 1831-32, Parliament passed the Slavery Abolition Act in 1833.
Most freed people had to work unpaid under an 'apprenticeship' until 1838.
Owners received £20 million, about 40 per cent of annual government spending; the enslaved received nothing.
War and emancipation.
By 1860 the United States held about four million enslaved people, mostly growing cotton in the South.
The conflict over slavery's expansion led to the Civil War, 1861-1865.
Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 declared enslaved people in rebel states free, and around 180,000 Black soldiers fought for the Union.
Formerly enslaved campaigners such as Frederick Douglass and Harriet Tubman became national figures.
After victory, the 13th Amendment abolished slavery in 1865.
Brazil, the last country in the Americas to abolish it, did so in 1888.
Abolition didn't bring equality: formerly enslaved people often faced poverty, segregation and violence, and Jim Crow laws kept Black Americans segregated until the civil rights era.
Legacy and action.
Around 60,000 Pacific Islanders were brought to Queensland's sugar and cotton fields between the 1860s and early 1900s, many recruited through deception or force, a practice called blackbirding.
Most still in Australia were deported after federation.
Their descendants, Australian South Sea Islanders, remain a recognised community.
Today, the International Labour Organization estimates tens of millions of people live in modern slavery.
Australia's Modern Slavery Act 2018 requires large entities, generally those with annual revenue over $100 million, to publish yearly statements on forced-labour risks in their supply chains.
You can look up how a company is responding.
Clothing, electronics, seafood and cocoa are often flagged as higher risk.
If you suspect forced labour, the Australian Federal Police accept reports; in an emergency call triple zero.
The key idea: Between the 1500s and 1800s, around 12.5 million Africans were forcibly shipped to the Americas, and enslaved people resisted throughout.
Part two. 1848: the year Europe caught fire.
In a few weeks of 1848, revolutions broke out in dozens of cities across Europe.
Kings fled, ministers resigned and constitutions were promised.
Within two years almost all of it had been undone.
A continent under pressure.
After 1815, Europe's great powers tried to restore order under conservative monarchs.
Austria's Prince Metternich symbolised the system of censorship, secret police and suspicion of change.
Beneath the surface pressures were building.
Liberals wanted constitutions, elected parliaments and a free press.
Nationalists wanted peoples such as Germans, Italians, Hungarians and Poles to govern themselves.
Industrialisation was creating a new urban working class in grim conditions.
Then, in the mid 1840s, potato blight and poor grain harvests sent food prices soaring, followed by a financial crisis and mass unemployment in 1847.
Hungry, angry crowds and frustrated middle class reformers were a combustible mix.
The springtime of peoples.
A revolt in Palermo came first, in January, but Paris ignited the continent.
King Louis-Philippe banned political banquets used by reformers.
In February protests turned into street fighting, soldiers fired on a crowd, and within days the king fled to England.
The Second Republic gave all adult men the vote, abolished slavery in French colonies and created national workshops for the unemployed.
News travelled fast by rail, telegraph and newspaper.
In March Metternich resigned and fled Vienna.
In Berlin, after deadly barricade fighting, King Frederick William IV promised a constitution.
Milan drove out the Austrians, and Hungary under Lajos Kossuth won sweeping self-government.
In weeks, governments that seemed immovable gave way to demands that a year earlier meant prison.
The Frankfurt Parliament.
In May 1848 an elected assembly met in St Paul's Church in Frankfurt to create a united, constitutional Germany.
Its members were mostly lawyers, professors and civil servants.
They debated long and earnestly, drawing up basic rights including freedom of speech and equality before the law.
But they faced hard questions.
Should Germany include German-speaking Austria and its many non-German peoples?
And the parliament had no army or money of its own.
In 1849 it offered the crown of a united Germany to Frederick William IV of Prussia.
He refused a crown offered by an elected assembly rather than by fellow princes.
The parliament soon dissolved, and its remnant was dispersed by troops.
Why the revolutions failed.
The revolutions failed for several connected reasons.
Middle class liberals wanted constitutions and order, while workers wanted jobs and social change, and the two soon feared each other.
In Paris, closing the national workshops sparked the bloody June Days uprising, crushed by the army with thousands killed.
Nationalities quarrelled too: Hungarians demanded freedom from Austria while denying it to Croats and Romanians within Hungary.
Above all, the armies mostly stayed loyal to their monarchs.
In late 1848 Austrian troops retook Vienna, and young Franz Joseph became emperor.
In 1849 Russian troops helped crush Hungary.
In France, voters elected Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte president, and in 1851 he seized power and soon declared himself emperor.
What survived.
Some changes endured.
In the Austrian Empire, peasants were freed from compulsory labour owed to landlords, and this was never reversed.
Prussia kept a limited constitution and parliament.
Denmark became a constitutional monarchy in 1849, the Netherlands liberalised its constitution, and Switzerland adopted a federal constitution.
Piedmont-Sardinia kept its constitution and later led Italian unification.
Rulers learned that ignoring public opinion was dangerous, and increasingly used nationalism for their own ends, as Bismarck later did.
Thousands of exiled Germans, the Forty-Eighters, emigrated to the United States, some later fighting for the Union.
Britain's Chartists held a huge London meeting in April 1848 but fizzled out.
The Communist Manifesto appeared in February 1848 but had little influence that year.
The key idea: Repressive rule, new ideas and a hunger crisis combined to make Europe ready to explode in 1848.
Part three. The Russian Revolution.
In 1917 Russia's tsar fell, and within months the world's first communist state was born.
Its shadow lasted the rest of the century.
Tsar to collapse.
In 1900, Tsar Nicholas II ruled the world's largest country with almost unlimited power.
Most people were poor peasants, still burdened by payments for land since serfdom ended in 1861.
City factories were crowded and harsh, and Marxist groups grew underground.
In 1905, troops fired on peaceful protesters in St Petersburg on 'Bloody Sunday'.
The tsar responded to the uprising that followed by allowing an elected parliament, the Duma, but kept most of his power.
Then came World War I. Millions of Russians became casualties, food and fuel ran short and prices soared.
In February 1917, bread riots in Petrograd spread, soldiers joined the protesters, and the tsar abdicated.
Bolsheviks seize power.
The Provisional Government kept fighting the unpopular war.
Vladimir Lenin, leader of the Bolsheviks, returned with German help, promising 'peace, land and bread'.
Germany hoped he would knock Russia out of the war.
In October 1917, November in the Western calendar, the Bolsheviks seized Petrograd with little bloodshed.
In March 1918 they quit the war, ceding huge territories to Germany.
A civil war followed.
The Whites, monarchists, liberals and some socialists, fought the Red Army organised by Leon Trotsky.
Britain, France, the US and Japan sent troops, and a few Australians served in northern Russia in 1919.
In July 1918 the Bolsheviks shot the tsar and his family.
The Reds won, helped by their hold on the heartland and railways, but millions died.
The USSR was formed in December 1922.
Lenin's one-party state.
The Bolsheviks moved fast to secure power.
In December 1917 they created a secret police, the Cheka.
In elections for a Constituent Assembly, they won only about a quarter of the vote, so when it met in January 1918 they closed it after a single day.
Rival parties and independent newspapers were banned.
During the civil war, 'War Communism' seized grain from peasants.
In 1921, sailors at Kronstadt, once revolutionary heroes, rebelled and were crushed.
Lenin then allowed some private trade again under the New Economic Policy.
Stalin's terror.
Lenin died in 1924.
Joseph Stalin outmanoeuvred his rivals and exiled Trotsky, who was later murdered in Mexico.
From 1928, Stalin forced peasants onto collective farms and drove rapid industrialisation through five-year plans.
Collectivisation caused catastrophic famines in 1932-33.
In Ukraine millions died, an event Ukrainians call the Holodomor.
In the Great Terror of 1936-38, hundreds of thousands were executed, including many senior communists and army officers, and millions passed through the Gulag labour camps.
Yet the Soviet Union also became an industrial power.
Superpower and legacy.
In 1941 Nazi Germany invaded.
The Eastern Front was the deadliest of World War II, and the USSR lost roughly 27 million people.
After Stalingrad turned the tide, the Red Army reached Berlin in 1945.
The USSR then dominated Eastern Europe, built nuclear weapons and launched Sputnik in 1957.
Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space in 1961.
Literacy grew, but censorship and surveillance were constant.
The Cold War against the United States followed, and communist revolutions came in China, Cuba and Vietnam.
From 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev tried openness, glasnost, and restructuring, perestroika.
Instead the system unravelled.
The Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991 into 15 countries.
The key idea: War, hunger and protest brought down Russia's tsar in February 1917.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What set the Atlantic slave trade apart?
Answer. Its vast scale and its basis in race.
Question two. What economic troubles helped trigger the revolutions?
Answer. Failed harvests and a financial crisis.
Question three. What combination of pressures brought down the tsar in 1917?
Answer. War losses, hunger and protests that soldiers joined.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
